0.short_title: Strategy and Policy: Concept and Course

intro_paras: In the waning days of the Vietnam War, Vice Admiral Stansfield Turner served as President of the Naval War College. He saw a glaring need to revolutionize the curriculum in professional military education. Rather than training officers, he sought to educate leaders. Admiral Turner argued: If you attempt to make this a prep school for your next duty assignment, you will have missed the purpose of being here. If we trained you for a particular assignment or type of duty, the value of this college would be short-lived. We want to educate you to be capable of doing well in a multitude of future duties…. Your objective here should be to improve your reasoning, logic, and analysis. The Strategy and Policy Course embodies Turner’s mission to place education over training by challenging students to grapple with the complex relationship among policy, strategy, and operations, lifting perspectives above the tactical level while sharpening critical thinking about joint matters. Critical strategic thinking constitutes the hallmark of the Strategy and Policy Course. We achieve this goal through graduate-level interdisciplinary seminars employing a unique methodology built upon two core components: the study of foundational theories of war, and close analysis of historical and contemporary case studies. The Strategy and Policy Course uses this case-study approach, integrating a diverse array of academic disciplines, including history, economics, political science, and security studies, to assess both historical and contemporary conflicts. This methodology exposes students to historical case studies in which senior political and military leaders, as well as staff planners, struggle to use the military and other instruments of national power to achieve the purpose and objectives of the state in both war and peacetime.

The course emphasizes the vital importance of orchestrating multinational cooperation while integrating all instruments of national power. Moreover, it instills in students the awareness and ability to perform comprehensive assessments at all stages of a conflict, and to communicate such assessments with clarity and precision. Finally, the course challenges students to think critically about the full spectrum of conflict: from prewar planning and the decision to go to war, to wartime adaptation, conflict termination, and the ultimate transition to peace. After examining past conflicts in a disciplined way, students emerge better equipped to grasp the values of the profession of arms espoused by the U.S. armed forces. Students comprehend more fully the capacity of U.S. military forces to conduct the full range of operations in pursuit of national interests. Moreover, students better understand why and how the U.S. military establishment is organized to plan, execute, and sustain joint, interagency, and multinational operations.
learning_html:
Program Learning Outcomes (CNW / NCC, JPME II)
  • PLO 1. Demonstrate joint-warfighting leadership when integrating the instruments of national power across the continuum of competition.
  • PLO 2. Create national security strategies designed for contemporary and future security environments.
  • PLO 3. Apply the organizational and ethical concepts integral to the profession of arms at the strategic level of war.
  • PLO 4. Apply theory, history, concepts of sea power, and doctrine through critical thought in professional communication.
Course Learning Outcomes
  • CLO 1. Evaluate, through Clausewitzian critical analysis, political and strategic arguments, and alternative courses of action.
  • CLO 2. Evaluate strategic principles, relevant theorists, and historical case studies to address complex problems of strategy and policy.
  • CLO 3. Analyze how various types of states generate and employ national power in maritime and other domains.
  • CLO 4. Evaluate choices of political and military leaders related to the origins, conduct, and termination of war.
grading_html:
Each case combines lectures, readings, tutorials, student essays, and seminars. Seminars run Even/Odd and are led by a practitioner and a civilian academic.

Final grade
  • Seminar Essay 1 — 25%
  • Seminar Essay 2 — 25%
  • Comprehensive Essay — 25% (distributed Thu 25 Feb 2027 0830, returned Fri 26 Feb 0830)
  • Seminar Preparation and Contribution — 25%

A final grade of B− or above is required for the master’s degree; C− or above for JPME I credit.

Seminar essays
  • Two essays, 2,600–3,200 words each (citations excluded), on questions listed in the syllabus; moderators assign the two questions at the start of the term.
  • Times New Roman 12 pt, double-spaced; footnotes or endnotes (Chicago Manual of Style); bibliography optional.
  • Use only syllabus readings and lectures unless the moderator gives written permission.
  • Essays are analytic “thought pieces” that argue a thesis — not research papers or narrative recitations.

Summary only — the syllabus governs (including grading standards, honor code, and the S&P policy on general AI / LLM use).
